text: The Gregorian calendar, introduced by Pope Gregory XIII through the papal bull Inter gravissimas issued on 24 February 1582, replaced the Julian calendar and is now used in most parts of the world. The primary change was a revised leap year rule: every year divisible by four is a leap year, except for years divisible by 100, unless they are also divisible by 400. For example, 1800 and 1900 were not leap years, but 1600 and 2000 were. This adjustment reduced the average calendar year from 365.25 to 365.2425 days, more closely matching the actual tropical year of 365.2422 days, thus correcting a drift of about 10 days that had accumulated since the First Council of Nicaea in 325. This drift caused the March equinox to fall before 21 March, disrupting the calculation of Easter, which is based on the vernal equinox. To correct this, the calendar was advanced by 10 days: Thursday, 4 October 1582, was followed by Friday, 15 October 1582. The reform also adjusted the lunar cycle used to calculate Easter, as astronomical new moons were occurring four days earlier than the calculated dates. Initially adopted by Catholic countries and their territories, including Spain, Portugal, the Papal States, the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, and France (which adopted it on 9 December, followed by 20 December), the calendar was gradually adopted by Protestant and Eastern Orthodox nations over the following three centuries. Greece adopted it for civil use in 1923, though many Orthodox churches continue to use the Julian calendar for religious observances. To avoid confusion during the transition, dates were labeled as "Old Style" (Julian) or "New Style" (Gregorian). The Gregorian calendar, like the Julian, is a solar calendar with 12 months of 28 to 31 days, totaling 365 days with a leap day added to February in leap years. The leap day is placed on 29 February, though historically it was inserted by doubling 24 February. Before 1969, the Catholic Church delayed certain February feasts after the 23rd in leap years, a practice still reflected in some masses. Gregorian years are identified by consecutive numbers, and a full date is specified by year, month, and day. The calendar cycle repeats every 400 years (146,097 days), consisting of 303 regular years and 97 leap years, resulting in a mean year of 365.2425 days (365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes, 12 seconds), equivalent to exactly 20,871 weeks. The reform was authorized by the Council of Trent in 1545, with Pope Paul III tasked to restore the vernal equinox to its 325 AD position and prevent future drift. Lilius proposed reducing leap years in centuries from 100 to 97, and Clavius expanded and defended the reform, advocating for a single, immediate correction of the 10-day drift. The 19-year lunar cycle was also revised to align with observed moon phases. The bull had no legal authority beyond the Catholic Church and the Papal States, requiring civil adoption for legal effect. The Spanish monarchy decreed the change on 29 September 1582, and the British Empire adopted it in 1752, followed by Sweden in 1753. Prior to 1917, Turkey used the Julian calendar for fiscal purposes, with the fiscal year starting on 1 March; from 1 March 1917, the fiscal year switched to Gregorian, and by 1 January 1926, the Gregorian calendar was adopted for general use. The secular difference between the Gregorian and Julian calendars is calculated by the formula D = ⌊Y/100⌋ − ⌊Y/400⌋ − 2, where Y is the year in astronomical year numbering (using 1 − (year BC) for BC years), and D is the number of days the Gregorian calendar is ahead. In leap years that are Julian leap years but not Gregorian, the conversion requires adjusting the date by one day less or more than the calculated value, with February given its appropriate number of days in the target calendar. The Gregorian calendar is proleptic before 1582, and the difference between the two calendars increases by three days every four centuries.

The Julian calendar is ahead of the Gregorian calendar. The secular difference D is calculated using the formula D = ⌊Y/100⌋ − ⌊Y/400⌋ − 2, where Y is the year in astronomical year numbering (using 1 − (year BC) for BC years), and ⌊x⌋ denotes rounding down to the nearest integer. For years that are leap years in the Julian calendar but not in the Gregorian, the rule is to add one day less or subtract one day more than the calculated value when converting to the Gregorian calendar, with February given its appropriate number of days. When subtracting days to find the Gregorian equivalent of 29 February (Julian), 29 February is excluded; thus, if the calculated value is −4, the Gregorian equivalent is 24 February. During the Roman Republic and Roman Empire, the consular year began on the day consuls first entered office—probably 1 May before 222 BC, 15 March from 222 BC, and 1 January from 153 BC—though the civil year consistently followed the order of months from January to December. In the Middle Ages, many Western European countries shifted the start of the year to Christian festivals such as 25 December, 25 March, or Easter, while the Byzantine Empire began its year on 1 September and Russia on 1 March until 1492, when it moved to 1 September. In common usage, 1 January was considered New Year's Day, but from the 12th century until 1751, the legal year in England began on 25 March (Lady Day), so events like the execution of Charles I on 30 January 1648 were recorded in 1648 because the year did not end until 24 March, though later histories adjusted it to 1649. Most Western European countries changed the start of the year to 1 January before adopting the Gregorian calendar; Scotland did so in 1600 (making 1599 a short year), and England, Ireland, and British colonies in 1752 (making 1751 a short year with only 282 days). In September 1752, the Gregorian calendar was introduced throughout Britain and its colonies via the Calendar (New Style) Act 1750. In countries where a legal decree sets the start of the year as 1 January, a specific date when this became standard can be identified; in others, the start of the year varied based on customs and influences. Neither the papal bull nor its canons explicitly fix the start of the year, though the canons state that the "Golden number" of 1752 ends in December and a new year (and new Golden number) begins in January 1753. Between 1582 and 1923, when the last European country adopted the Gregorian calendar, dual dating such as "10/21 February 1750/51" was common to account for differing year starts. "Old Style" (O.S.) and "New Style" (N.S.) denote dating systems before and after calendar changes, typically from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar between 1582 and the early 20th century. In England, Wales, Ireland, and British colonies, two changes occurred in 1752: the start of the year shifted from 25 March to 1 January, and the Julian calendar was replaced by the Gregorian calendar, removing 11 days from the September 1752 calendar. Writers used dual dating to reflect both calendar systems. In countries like Russia, where no year start adjustment occurred, O.S. and N.S. simply indicate the Julian and Gregorian systems; many Eastern Orthodox countries still use the Julian calendar for religious purposes. Extending the Gregorian calendar backward to dates before its official adoption produces a proleptic calendar, which should be used cautiously. For events before 15 October 1582, dates are generally shown as they appeared in the Julian calendar with the year starting on 1 January, without conversion to a Gregorian equivalent. For example, the Battle of Agincourt is universally considered to have occurred on 25 October 1415. Between 15 October 1582 and 14 September 1752, confusion arises in English-language texts when the same event has different dates (and possibly different year numbers) due to the use of Gregorian dates in continental Europe and Julian dates in English sources; events on the Continent are usually reported in English histories using the local calendar, such as the Battle of Blenheim on 13 August 1704. However, confusion can occur when an event affects both regions, such as William III of England sailing from the Netherlands on 11 November 1688 (Gregorian) and arriving in England on 5 November 1688 (Julian). The Gregorian calendar retains the Julian months with Latinate names and irregular day counts. Europeans often use mnemonics like "Thirty days hath September" to remember the number of days in each month, with variations in English, Italian, French, and Portuguese, and a version from c. 1425 in English marginalia: "Thirti dayes hath novembir / April june and Septembir. / Of xxviij is but oon / And alle the remenaunt xxx and j." A common alternative is the knuckle mnemonic, using the knuckles of the hands to represent months with 31 days and the spaces between them for months with fewer days. A similar method involves moving up a piano keyboard from an F key, with white keys representing longer months and black keys shorter ones. The Gregorian calendar uses a system of weeks, with physical or electronic calendars showing the weekday for a given date. Calculating the day of the week is complex due to the irregularities in the Gregorian system. When countries adopted the Gregorian calendar, the weekly cycle continued uninterrupted; for example, on 15 October 1582 (Gregorian), the preceding date was 4 October 1582 (Julian). Opinions vary on the numbering of days of the week; ISO 8601, widely used, starts with Monday = 1, with Mondays in the first column and Sundays in the last; in North America, the week typically begins on Sunday and ends on Saturday. The Gregorian calendar improves on the Julian calendar by skipping three leap days every 400 years, resulting in an average year of 365.2425 mean solar days, with an error of about one day every 3,030 years relative to the mean tropical year. Due to precession of the equinoxes and movement of the perihelion, the error relative to the astronomical vernal equinox is variable, with an average interval of 365.24237 days implying an error of about one day every 7,700 years. The Gregorian calendar is substantially more accurate than the Julian calendar’s average error of one day every 128 years. In the 19th century, Sir John Herschel proposed a modification with 969 leap days every 4,000 years (instead of 970), reducing the average year to 365.24225 days and making the year 4000 and its multiples common instead of leap; though proposed repeatedly, it has never been adopted. Over thousands of years, the Gregorian calendar falls behind astronomical seasons because the Earth's rotation is gradually slowing (due to tidal acceleration and leap seconds), while the year maintains a more uniform duration. An image showing the difference between the Gregorian calendar and astronomical seasons displays the June solstice date over Gregorian years, with each point indicating the solstice date; the error shifts by about a quarter of a day per year. Centurial years are ordinary years unless divisible by 400, making 1700, 1800, 1900, 2100, 2200, and 2300 leap years. These corrections cause 23 December 1903 to be the latest December solstice and 20 December 2096 to be the earliest, with a variation of about 2.35 days compared to the astronomical event. Proposed reforms of the Gregorian calendar include precursors to the original reform.
